newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Red Cross alarmed over attacks on Afghan civilians.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross alarmed over attacks on Afghan civilians.

text.p: The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) voiced concern on Tuesday at what it called indiscriminate attacks on civilians by warring Afghan factions.

"The ICRC once again solemnly appeals to all parties involved in the long-lasting Afghan conflict to use their utmost restraint and take all measures (to ensure) that civilians are respected and their lives spared during the ongoing hostilities," it said in a statement issued in Kabul.
The ICRC cited shelling of Kabul in June -- blamed by the government on the rebel Taleban militia -- in which more than 80 people were killed and at least 200 wounded.
It also mentioned Sunday's government air raid on the Taleban-held eastern city of Jalalabad, which it said killed eight people and wounded 39, including 11 children.
The ICRC's deputy head of mission in Kabul, Thomas Gurtner, said the ICRC was closely following events in Jalalabad, where the organisation has three expatriate staff.

"We are facing not only a city like Kabul under constant danger of witnessing civilian casualties occurring, but now in recent times other places, notably Jalalabad, and in the future possibly other towns may be prone to military activities which will need total attention," he said.
The ICRC is helping hospitals and clinics in Jalalabad and supports two main hospitals in Kabul, where it also carries out relief programmes for 30,000 families.

Gurtner said the ICRC was exploring alternative supply routes for Kabul, but was trying to secure assurances from the Taleban that it would allow relief convoys to reach the beleaguered capital via the Jalalabad road.
Many civilians have fled from Jalalabad to escape the fighting, some heading for neighbouring Pakistan or other safer areas of Afghanistan, Afghan sources said.
More than 6,000 Afghans have crossed into Pakistan at the Torkham border in the last five days to stay with relatives in the city of Peshawar and nearby areas, the sources said.
A Taleban leader in Jalalabad, Mullah Muhammad Rabbani, condemned Sunday's air raid and vowed to defend the city's air space, the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) reported.

He said the airport was open for international flights to resume. At least three flights a day were coming to Jalalabad before the Taleban captured the city last Wednesday, prompting the ICRC and United Nations agencies to suspend their flights.

AIP said ousted Nangarhar provincial governor Haji Abdul Qadir, who fled to Pakistan before the Taleban seized Jalalabad, had flown to Germany on Tuesday for medical treatment. He had led a group of neutral factions based in Jalalabad.
